listenings.text: I have taken small groups on ten-day trips for about fifteen years, and I want to tell you the one thing that separates the people who enjoy a trip from the people who survive it. It is not money, it is not the hotel, and it is honestly not the language either. On a ten-day trip, something goes wrong roughly four times. A bag arrives late. A room is not ready at two in the afternoon. Somebody tells you the wrong time for something. And there is always one line on a bill that nobody explained. Four hiccups, and none of them is a disaster. What changes everything is the first thirty seconds after each one. Some people wait. They stand near the desk hoping that somebody notices them, and by the time they speak, the person who could have fixed it has gone home. Other people walk up, say what happened, say what they need, and go back to their holiday. Those two groups had exactly the same trip. Only one of them remembers it as a good one. And here is the part people do not believe until it happens to them: your English does not have to be good for the second version. It has to be quick.

I work the front desk of a hotel in Miami Beach, and the last morning is the one guests always get wrong, so let me save you an hour of your life. First, check out is at eleven, but your bags do not have to leave when you do. We store them for free until the evening, and almost nobody asks, so people carry a suitcase around the city on their last day for no reason at all. Second, ask for the final bill the night before, not on the morning itself, because that is when you have time to read it and ask about the line you do not recognise. Every hotel bill in this country has one, and it is almost always a fee that is perfectly normal once somebody explains it. Third, and this is the one I would write on the door if they let me, tell us the night before what time your flight is. If we know, we book the shuttle, we hold a late room for you to change in, and we have the bags at the door when you come back. If we do not know, we cannot do any of it. It takes one sentence at the desk, and it is the difference between a calm last day and a bad one.

paras: The itinerary was ten days: two in the city, three on the coast, a day trip on the water, and the rest with nothing planned on purpose. Four things went wrong, which is roughly the normal number for ten days, and not one of them was a disaster. What is interesting is not the four problems. It is that each one was solved by about two sentences of English, and that the first one was solved badly and the last one was solved in under a minute.

The bag came on day two instead of day one. At the airport the first attempt did not go smoothly: too much apology, too much story, no reference number written down. In hindsight the whole thing was one sentence long. My bag has not arrived yet, here is the tag, when can you deliver it to the hotel. The next morning the same conversation on the phone took forty seconds, because by then there was a backup plan: a shirt bought in the airport shop, and the number of the claim written in a note on the phone.

Day three was the hotel. The room was not ready at two, and the person at the desk had been on shift since six in the morning and was not going to enjoy an argument. The sentence that worked was not a complaint. It was a request with a reason: we have been travelling since five, could you store the bags and tell me a realistic time, and if the room is not ready by four, what would you suggest instead? The room came at half past three, and the woman at the desk found a late check-out for the last day, which nobody had asked for.

Day six was the boat, and it was the one that could have ruined an afternoon. Three sources, three times, and none of them agreed: nine on the phone, ten thirty on the website, cancelled according to a driver. Nobody was lying. The trick was to quote instead of arguing. The woman on the phone told me it left at nine, the site says ten thirty, and the driver told me it was cancelled, so which of the three is right? It took the manager about twenty seconds, and the answer went into a message so that it could not change again.

The last hiccup was a line on the final bill, and it was the cheapest problem of the trip because somebody asked about it. It was a normal resort fee, explained in one sentence, and it stayed on the bill. Ten days, four hiccups, and the takeaway is not that the English was good. It was not. It was quick, it was specific, and it named the person who had said the thing. That is a different skill from speaking well, and it is the one that decides whether you come home saying it was good, or saying what actually happened.

choices: To warn you that ten-day trips usually go wrong.
To show that the same four ordinary problems are solved by two sentences each, and that speed beats perfect English.
To explain how to choose a hotel and a boat trip in Miami.

items.situation: Your bag has not arrived. Say it in one sentence, with the tense that shows it is still not here.
tips: My bag has not arrived yet, and here is the tag.
Lesson 3: present perfect with yet. Not my bag did not arrive.

items.situation: The room is not ready. Ask for the bags to be stored, politely, with a reason.
tips: We have been travelling since five, so could you store the bags and tell me a realistic time?
Lesson 5 plus Lesson 7: could you, and since for the starting point.

items.situation: Say what happens if the room is still not ready by four.
tips: If the room is not ready by four, I will need something else, unless you can move us tonight.

items.situation: Three people gave you three times for the boat. Report two of them.
tips: The woman on the phone told me it left at nine, and the driver said it was cancelled.
Lesson 9: told needs a person, said goes alone, and the tense moves back.

items.situation: Ask about a line on the bill you do not recognise, without accusing anybody.
tips: There is a line here I do not recognise. Could you tell me what it is for?
Lesson 2 plus Lesson 5: the small print, asked for politely.

items.situation: Somebody asks how the trip was. Answer in three sentences, and do not stop at it was good.
tips: It was better than the last one, because we planned less. The only real hiccup was the bag, and it arrived on day two.
Lesson 1 plus Lesson 8: a reason and a comparison. That is the whole point of the block.
